subject: ela
description: Students demonstrate command of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. They apply correct capitalization rules (sentence openings, proper nouns, titles, the pronoun I); use commas, parentheses, and dashes to set off nonrestrictive and parenthetical elements; recognize the difference between restrictive and nonrestrictive elements; punctuate sentences correctly with end marks, commas in series, commas with introductory elements, and apostrophes for possession and contractions; and spell grade-appropriate words correctly, including commonly confused homophones. Every item embeds the full sentence or short passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Capitalize correctly: first word of a sentence, proper nouns and proper adjectives, the pronoun I, titles of works, days, months, holidays, and geographic names
Use commas, parentheses, and dashes to set off nonrestrictive and parenthetical elements in a sentence
Distinguish restrictive (essential, no commas) from nonrestrictive (extra, set off with punctuation) elements
Apply standard punctuation: end marks, commas in a series, commas after introductory words or phrases, and commas with direct address
Use apostrophes correctly for possessives (singular and plural) and contractions, avoiding apostrophes in simple plurals
Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, including commonly confused homophones (their/there/they're, your/you're, its/it's, to/too/two, then/than)

problemArchetypes.name: Capitalization correction
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'last summer we visited the grand canyon in arizona with my aunt rosa.' Which version uses correct capitalization? Answer: 'Last summer we visited the Grand Canyon in Arizona with my Aunt Rosa.' because the sentence opener, the proper place names, and the title used as a name are capitalized.

problemArchetypes.name: Set off a nonrestrictive element with punctuation
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'My oldest cousin who lives in Denver is flying in for the reunion.' Choose the correctly punctuated version. Answer: 'My oldest cousin, who lives in Denver, is flying in for the reunion.' because the clause adds extra, nonessential information and must be set off with commas.

problemArchetypes.name: Restrictive versus nonrestrictive decision
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'The novel that won the award is on the table.' Should the clause 'that won the award' be set off with commas? Answer: No, because it is restrictive; it identifies which novel and is essential to the meaning.

problemArchetypes.name: Comma and end-mark placement
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'After the long hike we ate sandwiches apples and grapes by the river.' Choose the version with correct commas. Answer: 'After the long hike, we ate sandwiches, apples, and grapes by the river.' because a comma follows the introductory phrase and commas separate the items in the series.

problemArchetypes.name: Apostrophe usage for possession or contraction
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'The dog wagged it's tail when the children's laughter filled the yard.' Which version is correct? Answer: 'The dog wagged its tail when the children's laughter filled the yard.' because 'its' is possessive (no apostrophe) and 'children's' shows plural possession.

problemArchetypes.name: Spelling and homophone selection
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'Your going to need (their / there / they're) jackets because (its / it's) colder than yesterday.' Choose the correctly spelled version. Answer: 'You're going to need their jackets because it's colder than yesterday.'

Easy.description: A single short sentence (one clause, roughly 8 to 14 words) embedded in the item. The task is to identify or select the one correct version where exactly one convention is tested and the error is obvious, such as a missing capital on a proper noun, a single missing comma in a series, or one homophone choice.
constraints: Stimulus is one simple sentence included in the prompt
Tests exactly one convention (one capitalization rule OR one comma OR one apostrophe OR one homophone)
Identify-level task: pick the correctly written version or the single fix
Only one error to find; no competing or interacting conventions

Medium.description: A compound or complex sentence, or two related sentences (roughly 15 to 30 words total), embedded in the item. The task requires analysis across two conventions at once or a less obvious rule, such as setting off a nonrestrictive clause, deciding restrictive versus nonrestrictive, fixing a comma after an introductory phrase plus a series, or choosing between two confusable possessive and contraction forms.
constraints: Stimulus is a compound/complex sentence or a two-sentence pair in the prompt
Tests two interacting conventions or one nonobvious rule (nonrestrictive punctuation, restrictive/nonrestrictive judgment)
Analyze-level task: choose or produce the corrected version and identify why
Distractors are plausible partial corrections that fix one issue but not both

Hard.description: A short multi-sentence passage (roughly 3 to 5 sentences, 40 to 70 words) embedded in the item that contains several convention errors or subtle ones. The task requires evaluation: judging which full revision best applies standard English, explaining why a punctuation choice changes meaning (restrictive versus nonrestrictive), or correcting interacting errors such as a capitalization error plus a misused apostrophe plus a homophone. Requires inference about intended meaning to punctuate correctly.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 5 sentence passage included in the prompt
Contains multiple or interacting errors, or a subtle convention where punctuation changes meaning
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision and justify the conventions applied
Requires inference to determine intended meaning before choosing punctuation

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student capitalizes common nouns or fails to capitalize proper nouns, treating capitalization as decorative rather than rule-based
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'last Summer we visited the grand canyon' or 'My Aunt and Uncle bought a New Car' instead of capitalizing only the sentence opener and the actual proper names

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student sets off a restrictive element with commas, or leaves a nonrestrictive element unpunctuated, not distinguishing essential from extra information
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'The novel, that won the award, is on the table' (restrictive wrongly set off) or 'My cousin who lives in Denver is flying in' (nonrestrictive left unset)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student omits the comma after an introductory phrase or omits commas separating items in a series
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'After the long hike we ate sandwiches apples and grapes' instead of adding the introductory comma and the series commas

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the possessive 'its' with the contraction 'it's', adding an apostrophe to the possessive
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'The dog wagged it's tail' as correct instead of the possessive 'its'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds an apostrophe to form a simple plural (the greengrocer's apostrophe)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'We bought three apple's and two banana's' instead of plain plurals 'apples' and 'bananas'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses the wrong homophone because the words sound identical, ignoring meaning and part of speech
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Your going to need there jackets because its colder' instead of 'You're going to need their jackets because it's colder'
